title: Building Agentic Applications w/ Heroku Managed Inference and Agents — Julián Duque & Anush Dsouza

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on Heroku's platform providing inference, MCP, built-in tools, and managed infrastructure as the substrate for developers building agentic AI applications. Heroku is a developer platform used by software builders across industries, fitting both developer_platforms and general_purpose. summary: The workshop opens with Julián Duque and Anush Dsouza introducing Heroku Managed Inference and Agents, part of the Heroku AI offering. Anush frames the product against historical technology inflection points, positioning Heroku as the 'Heroku of AI' by making it simple to attach agents and AI to applications. The core mission is to make every software engineer an AI engineer. Three primitives underpin the platform: inference (curated models), MCP for extending functionality, and PG Vector for embeddings. The trusted compute layer—Dynos—runs first-party tools with scale-to-zero capability. Users get started with a single CLI command, and the platform takes an opinionated, curated approach to models. The hands-on workshop deploys a Jupyter notebook template to Heroku with Postgres persistence. Participants provision Managed Inference as an add-on through the Heroku dashboard, selecting from text-to-text models (Claude 3.5, 3.7, 4), Cohere Embed for embeddings, and Stable Image Ultra for image generation. The chat completions endpoint is approximately 95% compatible with the OpenAI API, supporting standard parameters and streaming. The agents endpoint always streams responses because tool execution takes time. Built-in agent tools include dyno run command, postgres-get-schema, postgres-run-query, document transformation, and code execution in Python, Node, Ruby, and Go with on-the-fly dependency installation. Demos show the dyno run command retrieving real-time server date/time, code execution computing Fibonacci numbers in Node and Go, and tool chaining combining HTML-to-markdown with Python code execution to fetch and run the Euclidean algorithm from Wikipedia. PostgreSQL tools work only on follower (read-only) databases for security; users attach a follower database to their application via the dashboard. A solar energy database demo shows the agent autonomously retrieving schema, generating SQL, querying metrics, and producing a breakdown report, with optional Python code execution for matplotlib graphics. MCP extensibility is demonstrated by configuring a Brave Search MCP server through the dashboard, exposing web search and local search tools to the agent endpoint. MCPs run on one-off Dynos with scale-to-zero, just like built-in tools. The workshop also demonstrates deploying a custom Perplexity MCP to Heroku via a Procfile with an mcp process type, making it discoverable by the agent. MCPs deployed to Heroku are accessible externally through a toolkit integration endpoint using server-sent events with bearer token authentication, with OAuth support planned. A Jupyter-based MCP client using the Anthropic MCP package connects to the Heroku endpoint, lists available tools (Brave local search, Brave web search, Perplexity ask), and executes a web search. An OpenAI SDK demo confirms API compatibility by performing inference with the Heroku endpoint. The session concludes with resource links and extended platform access through the weekend, noting no free tier currently exists.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Heroku AI's mission is to make every software engineer an AI engineer by simplifying agent and AI attachment to apps
Three primitives power the platform: inference (curated models), MCP (tool extensibility), and PG Vector (embeddings)
The chat completions endpoint is ~95% compatible with the OpenAI API; the agents endpoint always streams because tool execution takes time
Built-in agent tools include dyno run command, postgres schema/query, document transformation, and code execution in Python, Node, Ruby, and Go with on-the-fly dependency installation
MCPs—both built-in and custom—run on one-off Dynos that scale to zero after execution, so users only pay for compute used
Custom MCPs are deployed to Heroku via a Procfile with an mcp process type and attached to applications through the dashboard
MCPs deployed to Heroku are accessible externally via a toolkit integration endpoint using server-sent events with bearer token auth; OAuth support is planned
PostgreSQL tools only work on follower (read-only) databases for security; write access requires deploying a custom MCP at the user's own risk
Agents can chain multiple tool calls together—for example, fetching a Wikipedia page as markdown then executing the extracted algorithm in Python
The workshop is structured in four parts: environment setup, managed inference, Heroku tools/agents, and MCP support

sections.title: Introduction and Workshop Setup
sections.summary: Julián Duque and Anush Dsouza welcome attendees to the launch and learn workshop on Heroku Managed Inference and Agents. Julián explains this is a hands-on workshop requiring only a browser, with content available for self-paced learning. He directs attendees to a workshop site and Slack channel for setup instructions.

sections.title: Heroku AI Overview and Mission
sections.summary: Anush presents Heroku AI's mission to make every software engineer an AI engineer, drawing parallels to Heroku's original simplification of Rails deployment. He covers the platform's opinionated model curation, agentic control loop with tools, three key primitives (inference, MCP, PG Vector), and the trusted compute layer (Dynos) running first-party and custom tools.

sections.title: Hands-on Workshop: Deploying Jupyter Notebook
sections.summary: Julián guides attendees through deploying a Jupyter notebook template to Heroku. Steps include accessing the workshop site, signing up or logging into Heroku, accepting a team invitation, and using click-to-deploy with a unique app name and password. The notebook runs on a Dyno with Heroku Postgres for persistence.

sections.title: Introduction to Managed Inference
sections.summary: Julián introduces Managed Inference as a service that runs AI models within the same infrastructure as the application, keeping data from going to third parties unlike direct OpenAI or Anthropic API usage. He begins explaining how to provision an AI model to a Heroku application.

sections.title: Provisioning Managed Inference and Workshop Structure
sections.summary: Julián demonstrates provisioning the Managed Inference and Agents add-on through the Heroku dashboard resources page, selecting Claude 4 as the model. Provisioning exposes environment variables for inference URL, inference key, and model ID. He loads the workshop notebook from a URL and outlines the four-part workshop structure: environment setup, managed inference (chat completions), Heroku tools/agents, and MCP support. A fourth environment variable, TARGET_APPLICATION_NAME, grants tool execution permissions on the deployed application.

sections.title: Basic and Streaming Chat Completions
sections.summary: Julián demonstrates basic chat completions via HTTP request to Claude 4, showing the JSON response structure with choices and assistant messages. He then shows streaming via server-sent events, first displaying raw event objects with delta content, then parsing chunks and rendering the accumulated response as markdown in Jupyter for a better user experience.

sections.title: Agents Endpoint and Built-in Tools Overview
sections.summary: Julián introduces the agents endpoint, which differs from chat completions by always streaming responses since tool execution takes time. He covers the built-in tools: dyno run command for executing Unix commands or scripts, postgres-get-schema and postgres-run-query for database interaction, document transformation (HTML-to-markdown, PDF-to-markdown), and code execution in Python, Node, Ruby, and Go with on-the-fly dependency installation. All built-in tools are natively supported MCPs, and users can extend the agent endpoint with custom MCPs deployed to Heroku.

sections.title: Demo: Dyno Run Command and Code Execution
sections.summary: Julián demonstrates the dyno run command tool by asking the agent for the current server date and time, showing how tools provide real-time context beyond the LLM's training cutoff. He then demonstrates code execution in Node to compute the 30th Fibonacci number, showing the generated JavaScript code with markdown syntax highlighting. He switches the tool to Go, showing the agent generate, compile, and execute Go code for the same operation, returning 233 in both cases.

sections.title: Demo: Tool Chaining with HTML-to-Markdown and Python Code Execution
sections.summary: Julián demonstrates chaining two tools—HTML-to-markdown and code execution Python—by asking the agent to fetch the Euclidean algorithm from its Wikipedia page, extract the Python snippet, and use it to calculate the greatest common divisor of 252 and 105. The agent autonomously fetches the page, extracts the algorithm, generates code, runs it on Heroku, and returns the result with an explanation.

sections.title: PostgreSQL Setup and Database Querying Demo
sections.summary: Julián explains that PostgreSQL tools only work on follower (read-only) databases for security, preventing LLMs from writing to production. He demonstrates attaching a follower database to the application via the Heroku dashboard and identifying the database name (e.g., Heroku PostgreSQL Aqua). Using a solar energy database with hourly metrics, he enables postgres-get-schema and postgres-run-query tools. The agent autonomously retrieves the schema, generates SQL, queries energy data for the last 30 days, and produces a breakdown report by system, even running additional queries for more detail.

sections.title: Adding Code Execution for Graphics and MCP Introduction
sections.summary: Julián notes that adding a third tool (code execution Python) enables the agent to generate matplotlib graphics from queried data, though more tools increase execution time. He then transitions to MCP support, showing how to configure MCP servers through the Heroku dashboard's configuration page. He demonstrates attaching a Brave Search MCP server as an application, similar to database attachment, exposing web search and local search tools to the agents endpoint.

sections.title: MCP Execution, Custom MCP Deployment, and External Access
sections.summary: Julián completes the Brave Search MCP demo by executing brave web search from the agents endpoint, explaining that MCPs run on one-off Dynos with scale-to-zero like built-in tools. He then demonstrates deploying a custom Perplexity MCP to Heroku via a forked repository with a Procfile mcp process type and click-to-deploy button, attaching it to the application. He shows the toolkit integration page, which exposes all deployed MCPs through a server-sent events endpoint authenticated with bearer tokens (OAuth support planned). Using an MCP client from the Anthropic MCP package in Jupyter, he connects to the Heroku endpoint, lists available tools (Brave local search, Brave web search, Perplexity ask), and executes a web search externally. He closes with an OpenAI SDK compatibility demo and shares resource links, noting extended platform access through the weekend and the absence of a current free tier.
